comments.author: @jonjohnson3027
comments.text:
I think the biggest factor is the limited arable land along the coast.

Early settlement in Oregon and Washington was driven by farming, and the Willamette Valey and east/south Puget Sound region has plenty. This drew the farmers, which in turn drew the city dwellers to serve and benefit from the farmers. The coast doesn't have very much farmland by comparison, so there weren't as many people attracted to the coast during the formative years of development.

Of towns along the coast, Aberdeen, Long Beach, Astoria, Tillamook, and Newport all have potential for large deepwater ports. In fact, Aberdeen (36 feet), Astoria (42 feet), and Newport (40 feet) all have deepwater facilities. But, because farming was limited, growth was limited. During the formative years, timber was a major industry in coastal Oregon and Washington, but the number of people employed in timbering wasn't enough to trigger compounding growth. When the timber industry faded in the 1990s, so did the population.

Today, growth is physically limited by geography. There's not much land between the sea and the mountains, and there are no strong transportation corridors between present population centers and the coast. While growth could expand somewhat into the mountains, that's politically unpopular due to a desire for environmental preservation.
